newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party faces historic defeat - polls.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party faces historic defeat - polls.

text.p: Mexico's ruling party risks losing its majority in the lower house for the first time ever and a leftist veteran is well ahead in the key race for Mexico City, according to polls ahead of July 6 elections.

A series of polls published on Wednesday and Thursday, ahead of a Saturday pre-election ban on surveys under election law, were some of the last indicators of how Mexicans will vote in the key mid-term races.
Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, of the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), looks set to win the mayor's race in the huge capital city in a landslide.
Cardenas leads by an average of about 20 percentage points against his nearest rival, Alfredo del Mazo of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

A poll on Thursday by Indermerc/Louis Harris showed Cardenas winning an estimated 49 percent of the votes, once don't knows and abstentions were eliminated. His support grew by 4.2 percentage points since the same survey last month.
Del Mazo won 20.5 percent while Carlos Castillo Peraza, of the National Action Party (PAN) was third with 17.5 percent.
Other polls also showed Cardenas' lead growing, with a majority of voters saying for the first time they thought the left-winger would win.

Cardenas, the son of a popular former president, narrowly lost the contested 1988 presidential race but saw his support wane in recent years. Victory in Mexico City could propel him to the national spotlight once more, political analysts say.

Surveys also show President Ernesto Zedillo's PRI likely to lose its majority in the Chamber of Deputies for the first time since the party was founded in 1929. The PRI will keep its Senate majority no matter what the outcome.

A poll published on Thursday by Mexico-based Covarrubias y Associados showed the PRI likely to win 40.9 percent of the national vote, just short of what it needs for a lower house majority under Mexico's complicated electoral system.
"With the scenario of 40.9 percent the PRI would not reach an absolute majority in the Chamber of Deputies," said Jorge Alcocer, director of a magazine that sponsored the survey.
Two other opinion polls also showed the PRI falling short of a majority.

A survey published on Thursday by Mexico's Consultores Asociados had the PRI winning 31 percent support from voters, not including don't knows and abstentions. The PAN was second with 18 percent as was the PRD.

A similar survey by the University of Guadalajara the day before showed the PRI winning 30.7 percent -- almost level with the conservative PAN at 30 percent. The PRD was in third with 20.9 percent support.

In six races for state governors, the ruling party is likely to fare better, polls show. Although its lead appears to be shrinking, the PRI is set to win at least four or five of the states up for grabs.
President Zedillo, whose term lasts from 1994-2000, has vowed the elections will be Mexico's cleanest ever.
